name: Vishwa Brahma Temple, Alampur
period: One of the nine Navabrahma temples of Alampur, of the Badami Chalukya period (7th–8th century)
summary: In the northern corner of the Alampur precinct, the Vishwa Brahma temple is the best preserved of the Navabrahma monuments after Bala Brahma, its walls and doorway a gallery of refined early Chalukya sculpture.

sections.history: Vishwa Brahma — Brahma as lord of the universe — is one of the nine Shiva temples built at Alampur by the Badami Chalukyas between the seventh and eighth centuries, and the most complete of them after the still-worshipped Bala Brahma. It stands in the northern corner of the precinct beside Vira Brahma, across from the site museum. Though it no longer receives worship and many of its carved faces were struck away in later centuries of conflict, enough survives to make it a favourite of scholars of early Deccan art. It is protected by the Archaeological Survey of India.
sections.architecture: The plan closely follows that of Swarga Brahma, without the entrance porch: a broad hall on carved pillars leads to a sanctum ringed by an enclosed circumambulatory passage, and above rises a curving northern-style tower capped by its amalaka, itself finely worked. Writers have compared the temple with the Galaganatha at Pattadakal. The sanctum doorway shows Gajalakshmi above and the river goddesses Ganga and Yamuna on their crocodile and tortoise; the hall's pillars bear flowing floral designs, and the outer niches are crowned with kirtimukha masks.
sections.legends: Sculpture tells this temple's stories. On the back of the sanctum the king Bhagiratha stands in austere penance to bring the Ganga down from heaven to earth. Elsewhere are Dakshinamurti, Shiva as the teacher, seated with one knee raised; Trivikrama, Vishnu taking his three world-spanning strides; and a boyish Kartikeya holding his peacock standard — among the finest images of the Alampur school. All are gathered under the name Vishwa, the universe, given to the Shiva whom tradition says Brahma worshipped at Alampur.
sections.festivals: As a monument, Vishwa Brahma keeps no festival of its own; Maha Shivaratri at the living Bala Brahmeshwara shrine and Navaratri and Dasara for the goddess Jogulamba bring the precinct its great crowds. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Allow time for a slow circuit of the outer walls: Bhagiratha's penance at the rear, the niche figures, and the kirtimukha crowns are best seen in the low light of morning or late afternoon. Then study the doorway, where Ganga and Yamuna ride their mounts. Vira Brahma stands next door, and the museum opposite holds sculpture from across the group.

visit.timings: The Navabrahma precinct is open to visitors through the day; as an ASI-protected site, hours and any entry charges for the precinct and museum should be confirmed locally.
visit.dressCode: Modest dress is appreciated across the precinct, which includes living shrines; remove footwear where asked.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed at the monuments; tripods or professional shoots may need permission from the site authorities.
visit.gettingThere: Alampur is in Jogulamba Gadwal district, about 25 km from Kurnool and some 220 km south of Hyderabad, just off the Hyderabad–Bengaluru highway (NH 44). Alampur Road railway station, on the Hyderabad–Kurnool line, is about 9 km away; the temple stands in the northern corner of the Navabrahma precinct by the Tungabhadra, opposite the site museum.
